newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Squeeze expected on interest income for NZ banks.
newsitem.headline: Squeeze expected on interest income for NZ banks.

text.p: New Zealand banks contending with an extremely competitive market and thin margins now face a fall in net interest income over the next year, industry analysts said on Friday.
The main culprit is an expected slowdown in the growth of the mortgage market.
A likely rise in the number of bad debts is also seen nibbling away at profitability.

Andrew Dinsdale, chairman of the banking and finance group of New Zealand accountancy firm KPMG, told Reuters that New Zealand banks had learned to cope with net interest margins that were narrow by international standards, by ensuring they got "fair pricing" for other services, and by cutting costs.

However, the New Zealand economy is currently in a trough and many economists have revised down their GDP growth forecasts for 1997/98. Dinsdale expected the low growth environment would constrain banks' asset growth in the year ahead.
"The last 12 months have seen significant growth in the mortgage market, which many banks have done very well from.
"But I think we'll see that slowing over the next 12 months, so we won't see the growth in assets that has been compensating the reduction in margins," Dinsdale said.
"We'll see a reduction in net interest income."
Greg Tucker, banking analyst with ANZ Securities in Melbourne, agreed net interest income was likely to drop but said many banks were stepping up their fees.
"You should expect some increase in non-interest income, and maybe that will offset the drop in interest income," he said.

Tucker said insurance companies were entering the New Zealand mortgage market in an aggressive manner. Players such as AMP Group's telephone banking subsidiary Ergo Personal Financial Services, and National Mutual's answer to Ergo, Freedom Financial Services, could afford to lead interest rates lower as they were not burdened with costly branch networks.

"You'd expect those players not to be so much affected by it (the fall in net interest income) because they will get market share. But with the others that haven't followed them down you'd expect some shortfall," Tucker said.

David Tripe, senior lecturer at Massey University's centre for banking studies, disagreed with Tucker's expectation of a rise in income from non-interest income, saying the trend had been falling rather than growing.
He said while net interest income might be in line for a small fall, it still looked stable relative to assets.

"What is happening though, that will have an impact on bank profitability, is that there is going to be some increase in doubtful debts," Tripe said. He said all figures he had seen for the March quarter pointed to higher levels of impaired assets in New Zealand banks.

Tripe stressed that New Zealand banks' profitability was "not that bad", and said while the New Zealand industry had not achieved the cost-to-income ratios seen in Australia, its cost-to-assets ratios were lower than Australian banks'.
Four major New Zealand banks are owned by Australian parents. National Australia Bank owns the Bank of New Zealand group, and the Commonwealth Bank of Australia owns ASB Bank.
Westpac Banking Corp owns WestpacTrust in NZ, while ANZ New Zealand is an arm of the Australia and New Zealand Banking Group. The National Bank of New Zealand is owned by Britain's Lloyd's TSB.
